title: How to Start a Merchant Cash Advance Business in 2026
summary: Learn how to start a merchant cash advance business in the US, from choosing a funder, ISO, or syndication model to registering by state and building compliant underwriting and pricing. The guide covers Texas HB 700, Virginia and Connecticut registration, New York and California disclosures, and lessons from recent FTC and New York AG cases.
body_markdown:
To start a merchant cash advance business, choose a model (direct funder, ISO/broker, or syndicate). Next, form an entity and have counsel draft a true receivables-purchase agreement. Then register in the states that require it, line up capital, and build underwriting, pricing, and servicing workflows that hold up to regulators and courts.


This guide walks through each step as of October 2026, with the legal and operational details that separate durable MCA companies from enforcement headlines.


Demand is real. In the Federal Reserve Banks'[2026 employer firms report](https://www.fedsmallbusiness.org/-/media/project/clevelandfedtenant/fsbsite/reports/2026/2026-report-on-employer-firms/2026-report-on-employer-firms.pdf) , 8% of surveyed firms applied for a merchant cash advance in the prior 12 months. That figure reflects application activity among firms with 1 to 499 employees, so treat it as a demand signal rather than a market size.


This article is general information and is not legal advice. MCA rules depend on where each merchant is located, so work with counsel before you fund your first deal.


### Understand What a Merchant Cash Advance Business Really Sells


An MCA company buys a share of a merchant's future sales. The[FTC](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2021/04/cash-advance-firm-pay-98m-settle-ftc-complaint-it-overcharged-small-businesses) has described an MCA as money paid up front "in exchange for a larger amount repaid through daily automatic payments."


#### Price Every Deal With a Factor Rate and a Holdback


The factor rate is the multiplier that sets the total amount the merchant delivers. In a hypothetical deal, a funder advances $50,000 at a 1.3 factor rate and purchases $65,000 of future receivables. The holdback is the percentage of sales the funder collects until that purchased amount is delivered.


Some funders collect a fixed daily or weekly payment instead of a true percentage.[Connecticut Public Act 23-201](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2023/act/Pa/pdf/2023PA-00201-R00SB-01032-PA.PDF) covers that structure when it includes a reconciliation process. That process must adjust the payment to "a percentage of sales or revenue."


#### Protect the Purchase Structure With Real Reconciliation


An MCA is structured as a purchase of receivables, but courts look at substance over labels.[LP Legal](https://www.lplegal.com/content/recharacterization-merchant-cash-advance-agreements-bankruptcy/) summarizes three factors courts weigh. They ask whether payments adjust to actual revenue, whether there is a set repayment term, and whether the funder has recourse.


These factors are a guide rather than a safe-harbor checklist. In[Fleetwood Services v. Ram Capital](https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9881111/fleetwood-services-llc-v-ram-capital-funding-llc/) , a federal court in New York found the funder "never conducted a reconciliation" and concluded the MCA constituted a loan.


If a court recharacterizes your deals as loans, state lending rules may apply to them.


#### Plan for State Rules That Change Every Year


No federal MCA-specific license was identified in the sources reviewed, but MCA funders are far from unregulated. The FTC has brought enforcement actions against MCA operators, and states keep adding disclosure and registration laws.


As of March 2026,[Venable](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/03/state-commercial-financing-disclosure-laws) counts ten states with commercial financing disclosure laws: California, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Missouri, New York, Texas, Utah, and Virginia. Other trackers list more states, so plan for at least ten and confirm the current list with counsel.


Texas Requires Registration by December 31, 2026


According to[Venable](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/03/state-commercial-financing-disclosure-laws) , Texas HB 700 requires sales-based financing providers and brokers to register by December 31, 2026. Registration runs through the Office of Consumer Credit Commissioner (OCCC). Texas has no de minimis exemption, and the OCCC may seek civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation.


The[Texas OCCC](https://occc.texas.gov/industry/regulated-lenders/commercial-sales-based-finance/) began taking Commercial Sales Based Finance registration applications through NMLS on September 1, 2026. Under the final rules, as summarized by[Manatt](https://www.manatt.com/insights/newsletters/client-alert/texas-occc-finalizes-rules-implementing-sales-based-financing-law) , applications require a business plan. They also require a filing for each 10% owner and each control person.


The same rules restrict recurring automatic debits for Texas recipients. A provider may not automatically debit unless it holds a valid, perfected, first-priority security interest covering all of the recipient's accounts receivable. Manatt notes most funders reportedly cannot meet that condition, so Texas deals may need a different collection workflow.


Texas does not cap MCA pricing, because the Finance Commission is barred from setting a rate or fee cap ([Venable](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2026/03/state-commercial-financing-disclosure-laws) ). Disclosure applies to offers under $1 million, according to[Manatt](https://www.manatt.com/insights/newsletters/client-alert/texas-occc-finalizes-rules-implementing-sales-based-financing-law) .


Virginia and Connecticut Register Providers and Brokers


[Virginia Code § 6.2-2228 et seq.](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacodefull/title6.2/chapter22.1/) requires both sales-based financing providers and brokers to register. Each pays a $1,000 initial fee and a $500 annual fee. Exemptions cover financial institutions, providers with five or fewer transactions with a recipient in 12 months, and single transactions over $500,000.


Connecticut required commercial financing providers and brokers to register with the Department of Banking by October 1, 2024, according to[Venable](https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2024/06/new-commercial-financing-requirements-become) . Its rules apply to sales-based financing of $250,000 or less.


New York and California Require APR-Style Disclosures


New York's Commercial Finance Disclosure Law, implemented in[23 NYCRR 600](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/regulations/final_financial_services/rf_finservices_23nycrr600_text) , covers commercial financing of $2.5 million or less and took effect August 1, 2023. Sales-based providers must disclose an estimated APR to covered recipients.


California's disclosure rules apply to offers of $500,000 or less.[Goodwin](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2022/06/06_13-california-finalizes-commercial-financing) notes the DFPI regulations require APR disclosures even for non-loan transactions such as merchant cash advances.


#### Choose the Business Model That Matches Your Capital and Risk Appetite


Your model decides who carries risk, who needs capital, and which registrations apply. An MCA company usually operates in one of three positions.


- **Direct funder:** You buy receivables with your own or raised capital, set underwriting rules, and carry the performance risk.
- **ISO or broker:** You source merchants and submit deals to funders in exchange for compensation, without funding deals yourself.
- **Syndication partner:** You co-fund deals alongside a lead funder and share in the performance of each deal.


Brokers can be directly regulated too. Virginia defines a broker as a person who, for compensation, obtains or offers to obtain sales-based financing from a provider for a recipient. Virginia, Connecticut, and Texas all require broker registration.

### Follow These Eight Steps to Start a Merchant Cash Advance Business


Each step builds on the one before it, so finish your legal groundwork before you raise capital or market to merchants.


#### Step 1: Pick Your Model and Target States


Decide whether you will fund, broker, or syndicate. Then list the states where your merchants will be located, because state law varies by the recipient's location. That list determines your registration, disclosure, and collection obligations.


#### Step 2: Form Your Entity and Have Counsel Draft Your Contracts


Form a business entity with counsel and an accountant who know commercial finance. Have counsel draft your purchase agreement, ISO agreements, and syndication agreements before you fund a deal.


Your purchase agreement should include a reconciliation process your team actually runs. The Fleetwood decision shows that a reconciliation clause that exists only on paper can undermine the purchase structure.


#### Step 3: Register and Build Compliant Disclosures


Register in every state that requires it, starting with Texas before the December 31, 2026 deadline. Build disclosure templates for each covered state, including estimated APR calculations for New York and California offers.


Track federal rules as well. The[CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/1071-rule/) issued a revised Section 1071 small business lending data rule on May 1, 2026, with a compliance date of January 1, 2028. Ask counsel whether your products and origination volume fall within its coverage.


#### Step 4: Line Up Capital That Fits Your Model


Direct funders can draw on owner capital, outside investors, syndication partners, or credit facilities. No reliable public benchmark for MCA startup capital was found, so build your funding plan from your target deal size, volume, and expected collection timing.


ISOs need far less capital, because funders carry the advance. They still need working capital for marketing, compliance, and registration fees.


#### Step 5: Set Underwriting Criteria and Pricing Rules


Write your credit policy before your first application arrives. Inputs to define include recent bank statements, time in business, existing advances (stacking), UCC lien filings, and owner credit.


Price each deal so you can explain the factor rate, holdback, and estimated APR to the merchant. Factor rates published by industry sources vary widely, so set yours from your own risk and cost data. No authoritative public default statistic exists, because funders aren't required to publish loss data.


#### Step 6: Build Merchant Sourcing Channels


Funders can source deals through ISO partners, direct marketing, and referral relationships. ISO commissions are quoted in "points," a percentage of the funded amount, and vary widely by funder and deal.


Vet every ISO partner before you accept submissions. Confirm each one holds required state registrations and follows your disclosure rules, because their sales practices can become your liability.


#### Step 7: Automate Document Review and Decisioning


Manual bank-statement review and industry classification slow down every underwriting decision.[Lendflow Automate](https://www.lendflow.com/lendflow-automate) plugs into existing platforms through APIs and ready-made connectors to remove that manual work.


Its Doc Analyzer extracts structured data from bank files, tax returns, and PDFs. Industry Map assigns NAICS and SIC codes automatically, and Trust Score returns an explainable composite risk score. Pair these with decision rules in Lendflow Intelligence so your team can grow volume without growing headcount.


#### Step 8: Run Servicing, Reconciliation, and Collections by the Book


Document every debit authorization and process reconciliation requests on a set schedule. Keep records that show payments adjusted to actual revenue when merchants requested it.


Review collection practices state by state. New York's 2019 amendment to[CPLR § 3218](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2019/S6395) bars creditors from filing confessions of judgment in New York against out-of-state debtors. Texas rules list filing a confession of judgment as a prohibited practice, according to[Manatt](https://www.manatt.com/insights/newsletters/client-alert/texas-occc-finalizes-rules-implementing-sales-based-financing-law) .


### Avoid the Pitfalls That Led to MCA Enforcement Actions


Recent enforcement cases show where MCA operators get into trouble. Each one offers a lesson for a new funder or ISO.


#### Learn From Recent FTC and State Cases


In 2021, Yellowstone Capital agreed to pay more than $9.8 million to settle[FTC charges](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2021/04/cash-advance-firm-pay-98m-settle-ftc-complaint-it-overcharged-small-businesses) . The FTC charged that it withdrew money from business bank accounts without permission and deceived merchants. The FTC alleged the company misrepresented funding amounts.


In 2024, a federal court entered a[$20.3 million judgment](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/02/court-enters-203-million-judgment-ftc-case-against-merchant-cash-advance-operator-jonathan-braun) against RCG Advances operator Jonathan Braun. A jury found he knowingly violated the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act by deceiving small businesses about funding amounts, and he was permanently banned from the MCA industry.


In January 2025, the[New York Attorney General](https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2025/attorney-general-james-announces-1-billion-settlement-predatory-lender) announced a $1.065 billion judgment and settlement with Yellowstone Capital. It included more than $534 million in cancelled merchant debt, and the AG alleged the deals were loans "disguised as merchant cash advances."


#### Apply These Practices From Day One


- **Disclose funding amounts accurately:** State the net amount the merchant receives after every fee.
- **Honor reconciliation requests:** Adjust payments to actual revenue when the contract calls for it.
- **Limit debits to authorized amounts:** Pull only what the merchant agreed to, on the agreed schedule.
- **Check stacking before you fund:** Review UCC filings and bank statements for existing advances.
- **Monitor ISO partners:** Audit their marketing and disclosures on a regular schedule.
- **Recheck state rules quarterly:** Registration and disclosure laws keep changing, so assign an owner to track them.


### Build a Compliant MCA Company That Lasts


A merchant cash advance business can meet real small business demand, but only when its legal structure matches its daily operations. Start with counsel-drafted contracts and real reconciliation, then register in Texas, Virginia, Connecticut, and every other state that applies.


Build underwriting, pricing, and disclosure workflows that you can explain to merchants and regulators alike. Treat the enforcement cases as a blueprint of what to avoid, and recheck state rules often. The funders and ISOs that last pair compliance discipline with automated, data-driven operations.


### Frequently Asked Questions About Starting an MCA Business


#### Is a Merchant Cash Advance Legal?


MCAs are widely offered in the US, but their legal treatment depends on how each deal is structured and on state law. Courts may treat an MCA as a loan if it lacks real reconciliation, a set term, or limited recourse, so counsel should review your structure.


#### Do I Need a License to Start an MCA Business?


No federal MCA-specific license was identified in the sources reviewed. However, Texas, Virginia, and Connecticut require registration of providers and brokers, and at least ten states require disclosures. Requirements depend on where your merchants are located.


#### What Is the Difference Between a Direct Funder and an ISO?


A direct funder buys receivables with its own or raised capital and carries the performance risk. An ISO or broker sources merchants and submits deals to funders for compensation. Several states, including Virginia, Connecticut, and Texas, require ISOs to register.


#### How Much Capital Do I Need to Start an MCA Business?


No reliable public benchmark exists, and the answer depends on your model. Direct funders need enough capital to cover target deal volume and collection timing, while ISOs mainly need working capital for marketing and compliance.


#### What Is a Factor Rate?


A factor rate is the multiplier that sets the total amount a merchant delivers to the funder. For example, a hypothetical $50,000 advance at a 1.3 factor rate equals $65,000 in purchased receivables. New York and California also require an estimated APR disclosure for covered offers.
